explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The writer says, "By this we can be sure that we have come to know Him: if we keep His commandments." Knowing Him shows up in how we live. It's not just something we say.

explanations.answer: If we feel close to Him
explanations.explanation: Feelings are nice, friend, but that's not what the writer points to. He says we can be sure we've come to know Him if we keep His commandments. Trusting a feeling is like trusting a batch because the kitchen smells amazing. Lovely smell, but you still open the oven door and look.

explanations.answer: If we learn all about Him
explanations.explanation: Learning about Him is good, but the writer doesn't make it the way we can be sure. He says it's keeping His commandments. Picture a stack of cookbooks to the ceiling and an oven that's never been turned on. Lots of knowing, zero cookies, baker.
Liar. The writer doesn't sugarcoat it: "…he is a liar, and the truth is not in him." Those are strong words, baker. They match verse 3, where knowing Him and keeping His commandments go together.

Beginner is a gentle guess, friend, and I'd love to hand you that one. But the writer doesn't call this person a beginner. He says the person who claims "I know Him…" and doesn't keep His commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in him.

Stranger is close in feeling, but it's not the writer's word. His word is liar. The person says "I know Him…" yet doesn't keep His commandments, so the words and the life don't match. And the writer says the truth is not in him.

Yes, baker. The writer says whoever claims to abide in Him must walk as Jesus walked. Jesus Himself is the pattern. It's like pressing from the original stamp instead of a blurry copy, and that's the one I want my cookies coming from.
The writer doesn't point to the prophets here, friend. He points to Jesus. Whoever claims to abide in Him must walk as Jesus walked. Jesus is the one to follow.

The writer doesn't name the apostles as the pattern, baker. He says, "Whoever claims to abide in Him must walk as Jesus walked." So the walk to copy is Jesus' own. It's like a recipe card: you don't bake from somebody's good batch, you bake from the original recipe.

True, friend. The writer says, "Beloved, I am not writing to you a new commandment, but an old one, which you have had from the beginning." Then he adds that this commandment is the message you have heard. They'd had it all along.

It's true, baker, so this one slipped by. The writer says, "Beloved, I am not writing to you a new commandment, but an old one, which you have had from the beginning." He adds that this commandment is the message they have heard. So it's an old commandment they've had from the beginning.

explanations.answer: The darkness is fading and the light is shining
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The writer says, "For the darkness is fading and the true light is already shining." Fading means it's on its way out, and already shining means the light is here now. It's like the kitchen at sunrise, with the dark backing out as the light comes in.

explanations.answer: The darkness is gone and the light is coming
explanations.explanation: Close, friend, but the writer flips both halves. He says the darkness is fading, not gone. And the true light isn't just coming, it's "already shining." So the darkness is on its way out while the light is here.

explanations.answer: The darkness and the light are at war
explanations.explanation: No war here, baker. The writer says, "For the darkness is fading and the true light is already shining." Nobody ever saw the dark take a swing at a light switch.

The writer says something different, friend. If anyone claims to be in the light but hates his brother, he is "…still in the darkness." Still in it. Saying you're in the light isn't the same as being in it.

False is right, baker. The writer says that someone who claims to be in the light but hates his brother "…is still in the darkness." Still in it, he says. Saying you're in the light isn't the same as being in it.

Yes, baker. The writer says, "Whoever loves his brother remains in the light, and there is no cause of stumbling in him." That's the other side of verse 9. Loving his brother and living in the light go together.
That's where the writer puts the other person, friend. He says whoever hates his brother is in the darkness (1 John 2:11). The one who loves his brother remains in the light. Light is the answer.

The wilderness doesn't come up in this passage, baker. The writer says, "Whoever loves his brother remains in the light, and there is no cause of stumbling in him." So the place is the light. Loving his brother and remaining in the light go together.

explanations.answer: The darkness has blinded his eyes
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The writer says he does not know where he is going, "…because the darkness has blinded his eyes." I think this one is heavy. It's a sad picture of someone walking with no sight, and the writer says it plainly.

explanations.answer: No one is showing him the way
explanations.explanation: The writer gives a different reason, friend. He doesn't say no one is showing him the way. He says the person doesn't know where he is going because the darkness has blinded his eyes. I think it's a heavy verse, and the reason is right there in the text.

Circles aren't in the text, baker. The writer says whoever hates his brother walks in the darkness and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes. The reason is blindness. I think this is a heavy verse, so it helps to stay with what it says.

Forgiven, baker! The writer says he writes to the little children "…because your sins have been forgiven through His name." Forgiven means the sins are dealt with, and it's through His name. That's good news worth writing down.
Counted is a fair guess, friend, but it's not the writer's word. He says their sins have been forgiven through His name. Forgiven is the word for the little children.
The writer doesn't use judged here, baker. He tells the little children, "…your sins have been forgiven through His name." Forgiven is what he says. That's the reason he's writing to them.
True, friend. The writer says, "I am writing to you, fathers, because you know Him who is from the beginning." He says it again in verse 14. The fathers are the ones who know Him.

It's true, baker, so this one got by you. The writer says, "I am writing to you, fathers, because you know Him who is from the beginning." He says it again in verse 14. That's his reason for writing to the fathers.
That's it, baker. The writer says, "I am writing to you, young men, because you have overcome the evil one." The young men have won that one. He says it again in verse 14.
A giant isn't who the writer names, friend. He says the young men have overcome the evil one. That's the reason he gives for writing to them in verse 13.
The king of Egypt isn't in this passage, baker. The writer tells the young men, "…you have overcome the evil one." That's who he names. It's in verse 13 and again in verse 14.

Strong, baker! The writer tells the young men, "…you are strong, and the word of God abides in you, and you have overcome the evil one." Strong and the word of God abiding in them go side by side. That's quite a list.
Humble is a lovely word, friend, but the writer doesn't use it here. He tells the young men they are strong, and the word of God abides in them. Humble sounds like something I'm working on.

Patient isn't the writer's word, baker. He says the young men are strong, and the word of God abides in them. I've watched cookies through the oven door for the whole bake, so patient isn't my word either.
Yes, baker. The writer says, "If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him." He doesn't dress it up. Loving the world and the love of the Father don't sit in the same heart.
Peace is a good thing, friend, but it's not what the writer names here. He says, "If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him." The word is love.
Strength isn't the word, baker. The writer says, "If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him." It's the love of the Father he says is missing.

The writer says the opposite, friend. He says all that is in the world, the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes and the pride of life, "…is not from the Father but from the world." So none of those three come from the Father.
False is right, baker. The writer says the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes and the pride of life are "…not from the Father but from the world." They come from the world.

explanations.answer: Whoever does the will of God
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The writer says, "…whoever does the will of God remains forever." The world is passing away, but the one who does God's will remains. That's the long view.

Knowing Scripture is wonderful, friend, but that's not what the writer says. He says "…whoever does the will of God remains forever." It's the doing. Kind of like how I keep stamping even when I can't quote the whole recipe.

Not quite, friend. The writer says, "…whoever does the will of God remains forever." Nobody has to be flawless to qualify. The same writer says in 1 John 2:1 that when someone does sin, we have an Advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the Righteous One. So the one who remains is whoever does God's will.
